paras: The hanging of Stafford's assailant at Columbus, Texas, was the killing of an unnamed man by friends of a son of Capt. Stafford on December 27, 1882, after the man was said to have shot young Stafford. The story survives only as a brief Galveston News special from Houston, reprinted in papers outside Texas among other crime news, and it gives neither the hanged man's name nor his race.

According to the Houston special, a son of Capt. Stafford was shot at Columbus on Wednesday, December 27, but was not killed. Some of young Stafford's friends then hanged the man the dispatch called "the would-be assassin." The item says nothing of an arrest, of where or when in the day the hanging took place, or of who watched it.
No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution of the men who carried out the hanging appears in the coverage.

The Washington National Republican printed the item on December 29 under a Galveston, December 28 dateline, in a roundup headed "MORE MURDERS. Another Terrible Chapter of Crime in the South and Elsewhere." There it sat between a Texas accidental shooting and a Columbia, South Carolina, murder, with no comment on the hanging itself. The Knoxville Daily Chronicle carried the same special on December 31 under the heading "Texas News," dated Galveston, Tex., December 27, and gave the day of the shooting as Wednesday.
Both versions repeat the wire's wording nearly word for word and adopt its description of the hanged man as an "assassin," without naming him or saying how his guilt was known.
